subjects.description: Flows, stability, SDEs, Fokker-Planck and the NESS the FEP rests on.
subjects.name: Dynamical Systems & Stochastic Calculus

skills.description: A continuous-time dynamical system is a vector field $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=f(\mathbf{x})$ on a state space $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. The solution $\phi_t(\mathbf{x}_0)$ is the flow: where the state lands after time $t$. Free-energy gradients later define exactly such a flow on belief space.
skills.name: State Space & Flows

skills.description: A fixed point $\mathbf{x}^\star$ satisfies $f(\mathbf{x}^\star)=0$: the state stops moving. Self-organising systems settle onto such equilibria, and an active-inference agent's preferred state is a fixed point of its belief-and-action dynamics.
skills.name: Fixed Points & Equilibria

skills.description: Near $\mathbf{x}^\star$ the flow behaves like its linearisation $\dot{\boldsymbol{\delta}}=J\,\boldsymbol{\delta}$, where $J=\partial f/\partial\mathbf{x}$ is the Jacobian evaluated at $\mathbf{x}^\star$. The eigenvalues of $J$ decide whether small perturbations grow or decay.
skills.name: Linearisation & the Jacobian

skills.description: An equilibrium is stable if a Lyapunov function $V(\mathbf{x})>0$ with $\dot{V}=\nabla V\cdot f(\mathbf{x})<0$ exists in a neighbourhood: every trajectory flows downhill in $V$. Variational free energy is the Lyapunov function for perception — beliefs descend it monotonically.
skills.name: Stability & Lyapunov Functions

skills.description: An attractor is a set the flow converges to from an open basin of initial conditions; a stable fixed point is the simplest case, but limit cycles and strange attractors also occur. Pull-toward-preferred-observations dynamics make the agent's goal an attractor of its generative dynamics.
skills.name: Attractors & Basins

skills.description: A Langevin equation $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=f(\mathbf{x})+\boldsymbol{\omega}$ adds random fluctuations $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ to a deterministic flow. Its stationary density solves the Fokker-Planck equation and links dynamics to probability — the bridge the Free Energy Principle walks across.
skills.name: Stochastic Differential Equations

skills.description: The Fokker-Planck equation governs how a density $p(\mathbf{x},t)$ flows under a Langevin system. Its stationary solution $p^\star(\mathbf{x})$ with $\partial_t p^\star=0$ is the non-equilibrium steady state a self-organising system occupies — the formal target of surprise minimisation.
skills.name: The Fokker-Planck Equation

skills.description: A non-equilibrium steady state (NESS) is a stationary density sustained by ongoing exchange with the environment rather than thermodynamic equilibrium. The Free Energy Principle casts an organism as occupying a NESS whose support is its set of characteristic states; remaining there *is* surprise minimisation.
skills.name: Non-Equilibrium Steady States

skills.description: Perceptual and active dynamics can be written as a gradient flow $\dot{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=-\kappa\,\partial F/\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}$ that descends variational free energy $F$. Because $F$ is a Lyapunov function, the belief trajectory provably converges, tying the dynamical-systems and variational accounts into one story.
skills.name: Free Energy as a Gradient Flow

subjects.description: Statistical manifolds, the Fisher metric, dual flatness and natural-gradient inference.
subjects.name: Information Geometry & Natural Gradient

skills.description: A parametric family $\{p_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ forms a statistical manifold whose points are distributions and whose coordinates are the parameters $\theta$. Inference then becomes movement on this manifold — a geometric reframing of belief updating.
skills.name: Statistical Manifolds

skills.description: The Fisher information matrix $g_{ij}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\partial_i\log p_\theta\,\partial_j\log p_\theta]$ is the unique (up to scale) Riemannian metric on a statistical manifold invariant under reparameterisation. It tells you how far apart two nearby distributions are in information terms.
skills.name: Fisher Information Metric

skills.description: For $\theta$ and $\theta+d\theta$ close together, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\,\|\,p_{\theta+d\theta})\approx\tfrac{1}{2}\,d\theta^\top g(\theta)\,d\theta$: KL is locally one-half the squared Fisher length. This is why minimising KL is a geometric descent and not merely an algebraic one.
skills.name: KL Divergence as Squared Distance

skills.description: The natural gradient $\tilde{\nabla}F=g(\theta)^{-1}\nabla F$ is the steepest-descent direction in the information geometry rather than in raw coordinates. Because it respects the Fisher metric it is invariant to reparameterisation, and it typically converges far faster than the ordinary gradient on $0<\eta<1$ step sizes.
skills.name: The Natural Gradient

skills.description: Information geometry equips a statistical manifold with a pair of dual affine connections ($e$-connection over natural parameters, $m$-connection over expectation parameters). Exponential families are dually flat, so $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ acts as a Bregman divergence and the variational free energy decomposes cleanly along the two coordinate systems.
skills.name: Dual Connections & Flatness

skills.description: Casting variational inference as natural-gradient descent $\dot{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=-g(\boldsymbol{\mu})^{-1}\partial F/\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}$ makes belief updating geometry-aware: each step is the steepest descent of free energy in the Fisher metric of the recognition density. This unifies predictive-coding dynamics with information geometry and explains their robustness.
skills.name: Natural-Gradient Variational Inference

subjects.description: AEP, capacity, rate-distortion, Fisher, transfer entropy, empowerment and Landauer. It groups concepts that learners reuse directly in later strata and in the SkillTree learning path.
subjects.name: Advanced Information Measures

skills.description: For an i.i.d.\ source $X_1,\dots,X_n\sim p$, the AEP gives $-\tfrac{1}{n}\log p(X_1,\dots,X_n)\to H(X)$ in probability, so almost all probability mass concentrates on the typical set $A_\epsilon^{(n)}$ of roughly $2^{nH(X)}$ near-equiprobable sequences. The remaining exponentially many sequences are individually so improbable that they carry vanishing total mass, which is why $H(X)$ is the per-symbol description cost in the limit.
skills.name: Typical Sets & the AEP

skills.description: A discrete memoryless channel $p(y\mid x)$ has capacity $C=\max_{p(x)} I(X;Y)$, the largest reliable rate (bits per channel use) achievable with vanishing error as block length grows. Capacity is a property of the channel alone: it is the supremum over input distributions of the mutual information, and the noisy-channel coding theorem proves rates below $C$ are achievable and rates above $C$ are not.
skills.name: Shannon Channel Capacity

skills.description: Lossy compression is governed by the rate-distortion function $R(D)=\min_{p(\hat{x}\mid x):\,\mathbb{E}[d(X,\hat{X})]\le D} I(X;\hat{X})$, the fewest bits per symbol needed to reconstruct $X$ as $\hat{X}$ within average distortion $D$. $R(D)$ is convex and non-increasing: tolerating more distortion buys fewer required bits, and $R(0)=H(X)$ for a discrete lossless source. This is the dual of channel capacity and frames perception as lossy coding of sensory causes.
skills.name: Rate-Distortion Theory

skills.description: For a parametric family $p_\theta(x)$ the Fisher information is $\mathcal{I}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}\!\big[(\partial_\theta \log p_\theta(X))^2\big] = -\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\partial_\theta^2 \log p_\theta(X)]$, the expected curvature of the log-likelihood. It lower-bounds estimator variance through the Cramer-Rao bound $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge 1/\mathcal{I}(\theta)$, so it quantifies how much a single observation locally informs $\theta$ - a local counterpart to the global Shannon measures.
skills.name: Fisher Information as a Local Measure

skills.description: Expanding the KL divergence between nearby members of a family to second order gives $D_{KL}\!\big(p_\theta \,\|\, p_{\theta+\delta}\big) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\delta^\top \mathcal{I}(\theta)\,\delta + O(\|\delta\|^3)$, because the zeroth and first-order terms vanish. Thus Fisher information is the Hessian of KL at $\delta=0$ and the metric tensor of the Fisher-Rao information geometry; KL behaves locally like a (non-symmetric) squared distance whose quadratic form is $\mathcal{I}$.
skills.name: Fisher Information from KL Curvature

skills.description: Total correlation (multi-information) generalises mutual information to $n$ variables: $C(X_1,\dots,X_n)=\sum_i H(X_i) - H(X_1,\dots,X_n) = D_{KL}\!\big(p(x_1,\dots,x_n)\,\|\,\textstyle\prod_i p(x_i)\big)$. It is the KL divergence from the joint to the product of marginals, is zero exactly when all variables are mutually independent, and measures the redundancy a factorised (mean-field) model would discard.
skills.name: Multi-Information & Total Correlation

skills.description: Transfer entropy from process $Y$ to process $X$ is the conditional mutual information $T_{Y\to X}=I\big(X_{t+1};\,Y_t^{(k)} \mid X_t^{(k)}\big)$: the reduction in uncertainty about $X$'s next state contributed by $Y$'s past beyond $X$'s own past. Unlike mutual information it is directional ($T_{Y\to X}\ne T_{X\to Y}$ in general) and is a model-free, non-linear analogue of Granger causality, making it the standard measure of coupling in self-organising and neural systems.
skills.name: Transfer Entropy & Directed Information Flow

skills.description: The predictive information of a stationary process is $I_{\text{pred}}=I\big(X_{\text{past}};\,X_{\text{future}}\big)$, the mutual information between the entire past and the entire future. It equals the sub-extensive part of the block entropy $H(T)$ - the amount by which $H(T)$ grows sublinearly - and upper-bounds how much any model can predict. It is a complexity measure: structureless (i.i.d.) and perfectly periodic signals both carry little predictive information, while rich generative structure carries a lot.
skills.name: Predictive Information

skills.description: Empowerment is the channel capacity of the actuation-perception loop: $\mathfrak{E}=\max_{p(a^n)} I\big(A^n;\,S_{t+n}\big)$, the maximal mutual information an agent's action sequence can establish with its future sensory state. It measures how much potential control the agent has over its own future and is an intrinsic, reward-free drive: states with high empowerment keep options open. It reuses the capacity maximisation of im_channel_capacity with actions as the channel input.
skills.name: Empowerment

skills.description: The information bottleneck seeks a representation $T$ of $X$ that compresses $X$ while preserving information about a target $Y$, minimising $\mathcal{L}=I(X;T)-\beta\,I(T;Y)$ over stochastic encoders $p(t\mid x)$. The Lagrange multiplier $\beta$ sweeps the relevant compression frontier; the data-processing inequality guarantees $I(T;Y)\le I(X;Y)$, so no representation can be more informative about $Y$ than the raw data. It formalises 'keep only the bits of $X$ that matter for $Y$.'
skills.name: The Information Bottleneck

skills.description: Landauer's principle sets the minimal thermodynamic cost of irreversibly erasing one bit at temperature $T$ to $k_B T \ln 2$ of dissipated heat, tying information directly to thermodynamics. In the variational free-energy view, free energy is measured in the same units as entropy/information (with $k_B T$ as the conversion factor), so minimising variational free energy is simultaneously a statistical and a thermodynamic optimisation. This closes the loop between Shannon information and physical work that the free-energy principle exploits.
skills.name: Thermodynamic Cost of Information

subjects.description: Dirichlet parameter learning, novelty, model reduction and structure learning. It groups concepts that learners reuse directly in later strata and in the SkillTree learning path.
subjects.name: Learning, Novelty & Structure Learning

skills.description: In discrete active inference the generative model is parameterised by categorical distributions (the columns of $A$, $B$, $D$, $E$). Because the Dirichlet is conjugate to the categorical, a Dirichlet prior $\mathrm{Dir}(\mathbf{a})$ over each column makes the parameters latent variables whose posterior remains Dirichlet after observing data. The concentration vector $\mathbf{a}$ acts as a vector of pseudo-counts: its sum encodes confidence and its normalisation encodes the expected categorical. This is the formal bridge that lets an agent treat \emph{learning} as Bayesian belief updating over $\theta$ rather than over hidden states alone.
skills.name: Dirichlet Priors over Model Parameters

skills.description: Learning $A$ means updating its Dirichlet concentrations $\mathbf{a}$ rather than a point estimate. After each timestep the agent adds the outer product of the posterior over states and the observed outcome, $\mathbf{a} \leftarrow \mathbf{a} + \eta\, \mathbf{o}\,\mathbf{s}_\pi^{\top}$, so that columns accrue pseudo-counts for the states believed to have generated each outcome. The expected likelihood used in inference is the row-normalised concentration, and the implicit logarithm is the digamma-corrected expectation $\psi(a_{ij}) - \psi(\sum_i a_{ij})$. Because updates are weighted by the recognition posterior, learning and perception are coupled: better state inference yields sharper likelihood learning.
skills.name: Learning the Likelihood A by Concentration Counts

skills.description: The transition tensor $B^{(u)}$ holds, for each action $u$, the categorical probability of moving from state $s_t$ to $s_{t+1}$. Learning it updates the Dirichlet concentrations $\mathbf{b}$ with the expected transition co-occurrence $\mathbf{b}^{(u)} \leftarrow \mathbf{b}^{(u)} + \eta\, \mathbf{s}_{t+1}\,\mathbf{s}_{t}^{\top}$ for the action actually executed. Because transitions are action-conditioned, credit is assigned only to the slice corresponding to the chosen $u$, so an agent must act diversely to learn the full controllable dynamics. This is what allows an agent to discover the consequences of its own actions, not merely passive correlations.
skills.name: Learning the Transition Model B

skills.description: The vector $D$ encodes the prior over the hidden state at the first timestep of an episode. Learning it adds the inferred initial-state posterior to its Dirichlet concentration after each episode, $\mathbf{d} \leftarrow \mathbf{d} + \eta\, \mathbf{s}_{1}$, so that recurring starting configurations become more probable a priori. Over many episodes this lets the agent internalise the base rates of its environment's starting conditions, sharpening early-trial inference. Unlike $A$ and $B$, $D$ is updated once per episode rather than per timestep.
skills.name: Learning the Initial-State Prior D

skills.description: The habit vector $E$ is a prior over policies that is added to the expected-free-energy term in the policy posterior $\pi \propto \sigma(\ln E - \gamma\, G)$. Learning $E$ increments its Dirichlet concentration toward policies that were actually enacted, $\mathbf{e} \leftarrow \mathbf{e} + \eta\, \pi$, so frequently chosen behaviours become cheaper to repeat. This implements model-free habit formation layered on top of model-based planning: habits amortise the cost of deliberation but can entrench suboptimal routines if the environment shifts. The balance between $\ln E$ and $-\gamma G$ is therefore the formal expression of the habit-versus-deliberation trade-off.
skills.name: Learning Habits E over Policies

skills.description: Beyond state-epistemic value (resolving uncertainty about hidden states), an agent can value resolving uncertainty about its \emph{parameters} - the novelty term. Formally it is the expected information gain over the Dirichlet parameters, $\mathbb{E}_{Q(o,s|\pi)}\big[ \mathrm{KL}[\, Q(\theta\mid o,s) \,\|\, Q(\theta) \,]\big]$, which scores policies by how much they are expected to sharpen $A$ (or $B$). Novelty is largest where concentration counts are low, so the agent is drawn to under-sampled state-observation pairings. This is the active-inference formalisation of curiosity directed at the model itself rather than its current state.
skills.name: Novelty: Parameter Epistemic Value

skills.description: Active inference operates on (at least) two timescales: states $s$ are inferred within a trial (fast), while parameters $\theta$ are updated across trials (slow). This separation arises naturally because the Dirichlet posterior over $\theta$ integrates evidence pooled over many fast-scale inferences, with a learning rate $\eta < 1$ damping each contribution. Keeping parameters quasi-stationary relative to states is what makes the variational scheme well-posed: if parameters changed as fast as states, the recognition density would chase a moving target. The regime can shift - for instance under a precision change such as 0.95 - but the timescale ordering is the default that stabilises learning.
skills.name: Fast States vs Slow Parameters

skills.description: Bayesian model reduction (BMR) evaluates, post hoc, whether a simpler prior would have yielded greater model evidence given the already-computed posterior. Because the posterior under a reduced prior can be obtained analytically from the full posterior and the two priors, BMR scores many candidate simplifications cheaply without re-fitting. Pruning a parameter (e.g. zeroing a Dirichlet count) is accepted when it increases the free-energy bound on log evidence, removing complexity that did not pay for itself. In active inference BMR is the mechanism behind sleep-like consolidation and the discovery of sparse, generalisable models.
skills.name: Bayesian Model Reduction (Pruning)

skills.description: Whereas parameter learning fits a fixed model form, structure learning changes the form itself - adding hidden-state levels, new factors, or new outcome modalities. A common scheme grows the model by introducing a candidate new state whenever current explanations are surprising, then uses Bayesian model reduction to retain the addition only if it raises model evidence. This expand-then-reduce loop balances the pressure to fit data against the complexity cost in free energy. It lets an agent move from a misspecified model toward one whose latent dimensionality matches the world's.
skills.name: Structure Learning: Discovering Model Form

skills.description: When several candidate models are entertained, Bayesian model selection compares their log evidences (approximated by the negative free energy) and Bayesian model averaging combines their predictions weighted by posterior model probability $P(m\mid o) \propto P(o\mid m)P(m)$. Selection commits to the single best model and is appropriate when one structure clearly dominates; averaging hedges across models and is preferred under genuine structural uncertainty. Both rest on the variational free energy as a tractable proxy for log evidence, so the same quantity that drives perception and action also adjudicates between whole models.
skills.name: Bayesian Model Selection & Averaging

skills.description: Active inference selects policies that minimise expected free energy, balancing state-epistemic value, parameter-epistemic value (novelty), and pragmatic value. \emph{Active learning} is the special emphasis on the novelty term: deliberately sampling observations expected to most sharpen the model parameters, even at some pragmatic cost. The two are not opposed but nested - active learning is active inference whose dominant drive is parameter information gain rather than goal attainment. A mature agent modulates the relative weight of novelty so that early in life it explores to build a good model and later exploits it to satisfy preferences.
skills.name: Active Learning vs Active Inference

subjects.description: Empirical priors, deep temporal and hybrid models, attention as precision.
subjects.name: Hierarchical, Deep & Mixed Models

skills.description: A hierarchical generative model factorises the world across levels, where the latent state at level $\ell+1$ parameterises the prior (and often the dynamics) of level $\ell$: $P(s^{(\ell)} \mid s^{(\ell+1)})$. Higher levels capture slower, more abstract or more invariant causes; lower levels capture fast, concrete sensory detail. This conditional structure lets the same observation be explained by a chain of nested causes, factorising an otherwise intractable joint into manageable conditional pieces. It is the architectural premise on which empirical priors, deep temporal models, and cortical-hierarchy analogies all rest.
skills.name: Deep Hierarchical Generative Models

skills.description: An empirical prior is a prior whose value is itself inferred - here, the top-down prediction $P(s^{(\ell)} \mid s^{(\ell+1)})$ supplied by the level above. Unlike a fixed prior, it is updated continuously as higher-level beliefs change, so context flows downward to shape lower-level inference. This is how hierarchical inference implements expectation effects: an ambiguous low-level signal is disambiguated by the contextual prediction descending from above. The recursive use of empirical priors at every level is what gives deep models their characteristic context-sensitivity.
skills.name: Empirical Priors: Top-Down Predictions

skills.description: Hierarchical inference is implemented by message passing: each level sends top-down predictions to the level below and returns bottom-up prediction errors to the level above. Under a Gaussian (Laplace) approximation these messages are precision-weighted prediction errors $\xi^{(\ell)} = \Pi^{(\ell)}\big(\mu^{(\ell)} - g(\mu^{(\ell+1)})\big)$, and belief updating ascends the free-energy gradient until errors are minimised across all levels simultaneously. Only the residual that a level cannot explain is forwarded upward, so well-predicted signals are 'explained away' and do not propagate. This reciprocal exchange is the computational core shared by predictive coding and discrete hierarchical active inference.
skills.name: Prediction-Error Message Passing Across Levels

skills.description: A deep temporal model is a hierarchy in time: high levels evolve slowly and each of their states unfolds, at the level below, into an entire sequence of faster states. Formally one high-level transition spans many low-level timesteps, so a single abstract cause (e.g. a word) generates a temporally extended trajectory (its phonemes). This temporal nesting lets the agent represent long-range structure without an unmanageably long flat state space, and it provides natural boundaries for sequence segmentation. Inference alternates between fast within-sequence updates and slower across-sequence updates, mirroring the fast/slow timescale logic of perception itself.
skills.name: Deep Temporal Models

skills.description: Hybrid models join a discrete active-inference model (good for policies and abstract states) on top of continuous predictive-coding dynamics (good for sensorimotor signals). The interface works by Bayesian model averaging: the discrete level posts a set of continuous hypotheses (priors over continuous causes), the continuous level evaluates each via its free energy, and the resulting evidences are passed back up as a discrete likelihood. This lets a symbolic plan set the target for a continuous controller while continuous outcomes inform discrete inference. It is the canonical scheme for grounding discrete decision-making in continuous embodiment.
skills.name: Mixed Continuous-Discrete (Hybrid) Models

skills.description: Within hierarchical predictive processing, attention is the optimisation of precision $\Pi^{(\ell)}$ on ascending prediction errors: high precision amplifies a channel's influence on higher-level beliefs, low precision attenuates it. Because the precision-weighted error $\Pi\,\xi$ is what updates beliefs, modulating $\Pi$ gates which sensory streams 'win' - the formal account of selective and divided attention. Precision is itself inferred (and can be set by higher levels), so attention becomes an endogenously controllable hyperparameter rather than a separate module. Mis-set precision is implicated in conditions ranging from hallucination (too-high prior precision) to autistic perception (atypical sensory precision).
skills.name: Attention as Precision Control

skills.description: Temporal depth in action means evaluating policies that are sequences of actions, scoring each by its cumulative expected free energy $G(\pi) = \sum_{\tau} G(\pi,\tau)$ to a planning horizon. As the horizon grows, the policy space branches into a tree whose size is exponential in depth, so deep planning demands pruning. Hierarchical and deep temporal structure tames this by letting high levels plan over abstract sub-goals while low levels fill in the details, factorising one deep tree into shallow trees per level. The horizon thus trades foresight against tractability.
skills.name: Temporal Depth & Deep Policy Trees

skills.description: Sophisticated active inference computes the expected free energy of policies conditioned on the agent's own anticipated future beliefs, $G$ evaluated over $Q(s_\tau \mid \text{future observations})$, rather than over states alone. This recursion - reasoning about what one will believe after acting and observing - enables genuine information-seeking detours and contingency plans that 'naive' inference misses. In a hierarchy it lets abstract levels reason about how lower-level uncertainty will be resolved by future evidence, coupling deep temporal structure to deep epistemic planning. The cost is a deeper recursion, again controlled by horizon and pruning.
skills.name: Sophisticated Inference over Hierarchies

skills.description: In a deep model the variational free energy decomposes additively over levels and timescales: each level contributes an accuracy term (its prediction error against the level below) and a complexity term (divergence of its posterior from its empirical prior from above). Minimising the total means every level simultaneously balances fitting the level beneath it against conforming to predictions from the level above. This nesting realises the free-energy principle across scales - the same objective governs a synapse, a cortical column, and a behaving agent. It also makes explicit that complexity at one level is regularised by the prior supplied by the level above, not by a hand-set penalty.
skills.name: Multi-Scale / Nested Free Energy

skills.description: When a higher level is itself uncertain among several causes, the level below should not commit to one top-down prediction but average over them, weighted by the higher-level posterior - Bayesian model averaging applied within the hierarchy. This yields a mixture empirical prior $\sum_k Q(s^{(\ell+1)}=k)\,P(s^{(\ell)}\mid k)$ that propagates higher-level ambiguity downward honestly rather than prematurely collapsing it. The same averaging is what couples discrete and continuous levels in hybrid models and what lets an agent hold multiple contextual hypotheses until lower-level evidence adjudicates. It is the hierarchical face of model averaging seen in flat model comparison.
skills.name: Bayesian Model Averaging across Levels

skills.description: Hierarchical predictive coding offers a process theory for cortex: superficial pyramidal cells are proposed to encode precision-weighted prediction errors carried by feedforward connections, while deep pyramidal cells encode predictions carried by feedback connections, with the canonical microcircuit implementing the reciprocal exchange. Precision is associated with synaptic gain set by neuromodulation (e.g. dopaminergic/cholinergic), linking attention to physiology. This mapping makes the framework empirically committal - it predicts distinct spectral signatures (e.g. feedforward gamma, feedback beta) for errors versus predictions. The correspondence remains a theoretical proposal under active test, not a settled fact, and should be held as such.
skills.name: From Predictive Coding to Cortical Hierarchies

subjects.description: Vectorised updates, logsumexp, sampling, amortised inference and reproducibility. It groups concepts that learners reuse directly in later strata and in the SkillTree learning path.
subjects.name: Implementation, Simulation & Scaling

skills.description: A discrete Bayesian update $q(s)\propto A[o,:]\odot (B\,q_{\text{prev}})$ is implemented as element-wise array products and matrix-vector contractions rather than Python loops over states. Casting the likelihood lookup, transition prediction, and renormalisation into vectorised form on contiguous arrays exploits BLAS and removes interpreter overhead, which is the difference between a tractable and an intractable agent for non-trivial state spaces.
skills.name: Vectorised Belief Updates

skills.description: Computing $\log\sum_i e^{x_i}$ or a softmax directly overflows for large $x_i$ and underflows for very negative ones. The logsumexp identity $\log\sum_i e^{x_i} = x^\* + \log\sum_i e^{x_i - x^\*}$ with $x^\*=\max_i x_i$ shifts the largest exponent to zero, guaranteeing at least one well-scaled term and no overflow. Every numerically robust softmax, EFE-to-policy mapping, and log-partition evaluation in an active-inference implementation relies on this stabilisation.
skills.name: The Logsumexp Trick

skills.description: On a factor graph, belief propagation computes marginals by passing messages $\mu_{f\to x}$ and $\mu_{x\to f}$ that are products of incoming messages times local factors, with marginals recovered as the normalised product of all messages into a variable. Implemented in log-space (using impl_logsumexp) the products become sums, and on a tree the schedule converges exactly in two sweeps; loopy graphs iterate to a fixed point that approximates the marginals.
skills.name: Message-Passing Implementation

skills.description: Gradient-based variational inference parameterises an approximate posterior $q_\phi$ and descends the variational free energy $F(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log q_\phi(s)-\log p(o,s)]$ by automatic differentiation, updating $\phi \leftarrow \phi - \eta\,\nabla_\phi F$. Because $F$ upper-bounds surprise, each well-tuned step lowers the bound monotonically - the same descent illustrated numerically from 3.11735 nats down to 2.82346 nats. Implementation hinges on a differentiable $F$, a stable learning rate $\eta$, and a convergence criterion on $\Delta F$.
skills.name: Variational Inference in Code

skills.description: When an expectation $\mathbb{E}_{q}[f(s)]$ has no closed form, a Monte-Carlo estimator $\hat{\mu}=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(s^{(i)})$, $s^{(i)}\sim q$, is unbiased with standard error shrinking as $O(1/\sqrt{N})$. The reparameterisation trick rewrites $s=g(\epsilon,\phi)$ so gradients pass through the sampler, enabling stochastic gradients of the free energy. The error rate is dimension-independent, which is exactly why sampling scales to high-dimensional latent spaces where quadrature fails.
skills.name: Monte-Carlo Estimators

skills.description: A particle filter represents the filtering posterior $p(s_t\mid o_{1:t})$ by weighted samples: each particle is propagated through the transition model, reweighted by the observation likelihood $w^{(i)} \propto p(o_t\mid s^{(i)}_t)$, and the set is resampled when the effective sample size collapses. It performs the same recursive predict-update as exact filtering (ai_state_estimation) but for non-linear, non-Gaussian models where closed-form belief updates are unavailable; resampling is what prevents weight degeneracy from killing the estimate.
skills.name: Particle Filtering for State Estimation

skills.description: Amortised inference trains a recognition network $q_\phi(s\mid o)$ - shared across all observations - to output approximate-posterior parameters in a single forward pass, instead of running an optimisation loop per datum. The network is fit by maximising the ELBO (minimising free energy) averaged over data, trading an up-front training cost and a fixed amortisation gap for $O(1)$ inference at deployment. This is the inference engine of variational autoencoders and scalable deep active-inference agents.
skills.name: Amortised Inference Networks

skills.description: Profiling attributes runtime to the actual hot paths - likelihood evaluation, the predict step, or the policy search - rather than to assumed bottlenecks, and benchmarking measures wall-clock against problem size to confirm the empirical scaling curve. Sound practice fixes inputs, warms caches, runs repeated trials to control variance, and reports medians; only after measurement should code be optimised, because intuition about cost in vectorised numerical code is frequently wrong.
skills.name: Benchmarking & Profiling Inference

skills.description: A reproducible simulation seeds every source of randomness from a single recorded master seed, threads explicit RNG state rather than relying on hidden global state, and pins library versions so sampler behaviour is fixed. Determinism is what makes a sampling-based result (impl_monte_carlo, impl_particle_filter) a scientific claim rather than an anecdote: re-running must reproduce the same numbers byte-for-byte, which also makes regressions and benchmark comparisons meaningful. This extends comp_determinism to the full stochastic pipeline.
skills.name: Reproducibility & Deterministic Seeding

skills.description: A joint state of $K$ factors each with $n$ levels has $n^K$ configurations, so exact inference is exponential in the number of factors - the state-space explosion. Modelling the generative model as a product of conditionally independent factors and using a mean-field posterior turns $n^K$ into roughly $K$ tensors of size $n$, trading exactness for tractability. The art is choosing a factorisation whose discarded dependencies (measured by total correlation) are small enough that the approximation stays faithful.
skills.name: Scaling Trade-offs & Factorisation

skills.description: An analytic gradient implementation is checked against the central finite difference $\partial_\theta F \approx \big(F(\theta+\epsilon)-F(\theta-\epsilon)\big)/(2\epsilon)$, with agreement to a small relative tolerance confirming correctness. The central scheme has $O(\epsilon^2)$ truncation error, so $\epsilon$ must be small enough to be accurate yet large enough to avoid floating-point cancellation. This numeric-vs-analytic check is the standard guard against silent gradient bugs in any free-energy minimiser.
skills.name: Gradient Checking & Analytic Verification

skills.description: The decisive test of a generative model is a round trip: sample latent causes from a known ground truth, generate observations through the model, run inference, and confirm the posterior recovers the planted causes within a calibrated tolerance. Following a real-data discipline, the test exercises the real sampling, inference, and convergence (impl_gradient_checking, impl_reproducibility) end-to-end rather than replacing them - a green test that never runs the actual update is worthless. Posterior calibration checks (coverage of credible intervals) turn 'it ran' into 'it is correct.'
skills.name: Testing a Generative Model (Round-Trip Discipline)

subjects.description: Shared generative models, precision attacks, trust, resilience and epistemic health.
subjects.name: Cognitive Security & Information Ecosystems

skills.description: An information ecosystem is a network of minds whose individual generative models $p_i(o,s)$ are coupled through shared observations (media, speech, sensors). Treating the ecosystem as a single distributed generative model lets us ask system-level questions: what hidden causes $s$ does the population infer, and how faithfully do its predictions track the world? Cognitive security is the discipline of keeping that collective inference well-calibrated against reality.
skills.name: The Information Ecosystem as a Shared Generative Model

skills.description: Members of an epistemic community share priors $p(s)$ acquired through common training, sources and discourse. Shared priors are efficient: they compress the space of hypotheses each member must entertain and make communication low-bandwidth. The same compression is a vulnerability - a prior held in common but poorly calibrated propagates correlated error, which is why healthy ecosystems preserve prior diversity.
skills.name: Epistemic Communities & Shared Priors

skills.description: Sensemaking is the community-scale analogue of perception: many agents pool evidence to estimate a shared posterior $p(s\mid o)$ over what is happening. Each contribution is a likelihood term; deliberation approximates Bayesian updating across the group. Robust sensemaking requires that contributed evidence be conditionally informative and that the aggregation rule weight sources by their reliability rather than their volume.
skills.name: Sensemaking as Collective Inference

skills.description: Two failure modes map cleanly onto the generative model. Injecting a false prior $p(s)$ biases inference before any evidence arrives; corrupting the likelihood $p(o\mid s)$ (fabricated 'evidence', deepfakes) makes genuine data point at the wrong cause. Both raise the divergence between the community's posterior and reality. Naming the target - prior vs. likelihood - tells a defender which calibration step to harden.
skills.name: Misinformation as Injected False Priors / Corrupted Likelihoods

skills.description: Precision is the inverse-variance weight an agent assigns to a prediction error; it sets how strongly a signal updates beliefs. Attention is precision allocation. An adversary need not change the data if they can change its weighting: amplifying the precision of low-quality channels or suppressing trusted ones reshapes the posterior. Defences restore calibrated precision - weighting signals by demonstrated reliability, not salience.
skills.name: Precision & Attention as the Attack Surface

skills.description: A narrative is a compressed story about hidden causes that also carries a prior $p(\pi)$ over which policies $\pi$ are sensible. Because expected free energy is weighted by this policy prior, a narrative steers behaviour even when the evidence is unchanged. Defensive cognitive security audits the narratives in circulation for which actions they make thinkable, and protects the plurality of available policies.
skills.name: Narrative as a Policy Prior

skills.description: In Bayesian persuasion a sender commits to a signalling scheme $p(o\mid s)$ knowing the receiver will update rationally. Framing chooses which partition of the state to make salient - both legitimate (clear public-health messaging) and adversarial uses share this structure. The defensive question is whether the signalling scheme is truth-conducive: does the induced posterior move toward or away from the actual state?
skills.name: Bayesian Persuasion & Framing

skills.description: Trust is the precision an agent has learned to assign to a source's reports, updated over repeated encounters as a hierarchical hyperparameter. Well-calibrated trust tracks a source's long-run accuracy; manufactured trust (astroturfing, borrowed credibility) inflates precision without the underlying reliability. Resilient ecosystems update trust on outcomes, making it expensive to spoof and quick to revoke.
skills.name: Trust as Learned Precision over Sources

skills.description: An ecosystem with calibrated priors and trust resists injected beliefs the way an immune system rejects antigens: a claim that fits the world poorly generates large prediction error and, weighted by appropriate precision, is down-updated rather than absorbed. Resilience is thus an emergent property of good calibration, not censorship. Over-reactive 'autoimmune' regimes that reject all novel evidence are themselves a failure mode.
skills.name: Epistemic Immune Responses & Resilience

skills.description: A sophisticated defender runs inference one level up: estimating the adversary's generative model, their assumed model of the target audience, and the policy prior they are trying to install. This recursive theory-of-mind turns defence into a POMDP where the hidden state includes the adversary's intent. The aim is to reduce the defender's uncertainty about the manipulation strategy, then act to neutralise it transparently.
skills.name: Adversarial Inference: Modelling the Adversary's Generative Model

skills.description: Calibrated priors, trustworthy sources and shared evidentiary standards are a commons: individually rational free-riding (spreading unchecked claims) degrades a resource everyone depends on. Governing the information commons means institutions and norms that internalise the externalities of low-quality signalling, preserving the conditions under which collective inference stays accurate. This connects cognitive security to multi-agent coordination.
skills.name: Collective Epistemic Security & the Information Commons

skills.description: Epistemic health admits measurement. Source diversity is the entropy of the source distribution; redundancy and capture show up as high mutual information between supposedly independent channels $I(X;Y)$, signalling correlated rather than independent evidence. Monitoring these quantities over time detects homogenisation and coordinated inauthentic behaviour before the posterior visibly drifts. The metrics are diagnostic, defensive, and content-neutral.
skills.name: Measuring Epistemic Health: Information-Theoretic Diversity

subjects.description: Stigmergy, swarm inference, shared blankets, niche construction and synchrony. It groups concepts that learners reuse directly in later strata and in the SkillTree learning path.
subjects.name: Collective Behaviour & Multi-Agent Inference

skills.description: Stigmergy is coordination through persistent modifications of a shared environment - ant pheromone fields, wasp nest geometry - rather than direct messaging. The environment acts as an externalised, slowly-decaying belief state that every agent both reads and writes. This offloads memory and inference into the world, letting a colony aggregate evidence across time without any individual holding the global picture.
skills.name: Stigmergy: The Environment as Shared Memory

skills.description: A foraging colony infers a posterior over where food is. Each laden ant deposits pheromone proportional to reward, so the evaporating field approximates a likelihood-weighted estimate $p(\text{location}\mid \text{returns})$ that the colony exploits and refines. Evaporation implements forgetting of stale evidence, and recruitment implements precision-weighted sampling toward high-value hypotheses - the explore/exploit trade-off realised in chemistry.
skills.name: Ant-Colony Foraging as Distributed Inference

skills.description: Coordinated collectives share parts of a generative model: a common model of the environment and, often, nested models of one another's states. When each agent's model includes a model of its neighbours, inference becomes hierarchical across agents, and consensus corresponds to the agents settling into mutually consistent posteriors. This nesting is what makes a swarm more than a sum of independent inferences.
skills.name: Shared & Nested Generative Models across Agents

skills.description: Communication is action in a partner's sensory space: an agent emits a signal expected to drive the recipient's posterior toward the sender's belief about a hidden state. Honest, informative signalling raises the mutual information between signal and state, $I(\text{signal};s)$, and is favoured when it lowers the dyad's joint free energy. This recasts the alignment of beliefs as cooperative active inference.
skills.name: Communication as Inference: Signalling to Align Beliefs

skills.description: When agents couple tightly, their individual Markov blankets can compose into a single blanket separating the collective's internal states from its environment. At that point the group is itself a thing that does inference - a superorganism - with its own sensory and active states. The colony-as-individual is not metaphor but a precise statement about the statistical boundary that emerges from coupling.
skills.name: The Multi-Agent / Shared Markov Blanket

skills.description: Swarm intelligence is decentralised inference: each agent follows local update rules using only neighbour and environmental signals, yet the collective computes a coherent decision. Robustness comes from redundancy and the absence of a single point of failure; adaptability comes from the same free-energy gradient acting at every node. The design lesson is that global competence need not require global information.
skills.name: Swarm Intelligence & Decentralised Decision

skills.description: Quorum sensing - in house-hunting ants or bacteria - lets a collective wait until accumulated local signals cross a threshold before committing. This is a distributed sequential probability-ratio test: the threshold trades off speed against accuracy, and a higher quorum demands more evidence before the group acts. It is collective evidence accumulation made physical, with the threshold encoding the cost of a premature decision.
skills.name: Quorum Sensing as Collective Evidence Accumulation

skills.description: Niche construction is the feedback loop in which agents modify their environment (trails, structures, accumulated culture) and those modifications become part of the generative model inherited by the next cohort. The environment thus carries priors across generations, extending stigmergy through time. Adaptive niches lower the free energy of those who inherit them; maladaptive ones lock in error - a structural risk shared with information ecosystems.
skills.name: Cultural Niche Construction

skills.description: Conformity arises when agents assign high precision to social evidence relative to private observation; herding and information cascades occur when each agent rationally weights others' choices and stops contributing private evidence. Moderate social precision is adaptive (cheap, fast learning); excessive social precision collapses diversity and lets early errors cascade. The same precision knob that enables coordination enables fragility.
skills.name: Social Conformity & Herding as Shared Priors

skills.description: In a collective, each agent's expected free energy includes terms that depend on others' policies, so policy selection becomes a coupled, game-theoretic optimisation. Epistemic value now includes resolving uncertainty about partners, and pragmatic value includes reaching shared preferred outcomes. Cooperative equilibria emerge when minimising one's own expected free energy also lowers the group's - the formal basis for self-organised coordination.
skills.name: Multi-Agent Expected Free Energy

skills.description: Pattern formation - from Turing reaction-diffusion to collective cell migration - can be read as a population of agents inferring and acting to realise a target configuration encoded as prior preferences. Each cell senses local signals and adjusts state and position to reduce prediction error against the morphological prior. Development thereby becomes large-scale active inference, and regeneration becomes re-inference after perturbation.
skills.name: Morphogenesis & Pattern Formation as Inference

skills.description: When agents are reciprocally coupled, their internal states can enter generalised synchrony: a smooth functional relationship between trajectories, the dynamical-systems signature of two systems inferring each other. This underlies turn-taking, joint attention and flocking, and is the substrate on which all the preceding skills - stigmergy, communication, shared blankets - ultimately rest. Coordination, at base, is coupled minds achieving synchrony of belief.
skills.name: Generalised Synchrony across Coupled Agents

subjects.description: Factor graphs, sum-product, belief propagation, variational message passing and loopy propagation as one connected computational ladder.
subjects.name: Message Passing on Factor Graphs

skills.description: A factor graph draws variables and factors as two kinds of nodes, with an edge wherever a factor depends on a variable. It makes the conditional-independence structure of a model explicit: the absence of an edge is a modelling commitment that two quantities interact only through the variables they share.
skills.name: Factor Graphs and Conditional Independence

skills.description: Sum-product computes a variable's marginal as the product of incoming messages from its neighbouring factors, where each factor message sums out the other variables it touches. On a tree the schedule is exact and each message is reused by every marginal that needs it, turning a global sum into local work.
skills.name: The Sum-Product Algorithm

skills.description: Belief propagation is sum-product organised as a leaf-to-root then root-to-leaf sweep, so a single pass in each direction yields every variable's marginal. The belief at a node is its local evidence times the product of stabilised incoming messages, which is why the schedule terminates exactly on an acyclic graph. On a worked three-node sticky chain, a single informative reading at the middle node (posterior 0.9) propagates outward and lifts each unobserved neighbour to 0.74, a smoothing lift of 0.24 above an even prior — and these marginals match a brute-force enumeration of the full joint exactly.
skills.name: Belief Propagation on Trees

skills.description: Variational message passing recasts mean-field coordinate ascent as messages: each factor sends expected sufficient statistics to its neighbours, and a variable updates its approximate posterior from the messages it receives. It extends exact propagation to intractable models by optimising a bound instead of computing exact marginals.
skills.name: Variational Message Passing

skills.description: Running belief propagation on a graph with cycles drops the exactness guarantee: messages may oscillate or settle on an approximate fixed point that corresponds to a stationary point of the Bethe free energy. Practitioners damp updates and monitor convergence rather than assuming the returned beliefs are true marginals.
skills.name: Loopy Belief Propagation and Convergence

subjects.description: Precision as unified confidence control, entropy-regularised exploration, the explore-exploit frontier, and risk-sensitive guidance functions.
subjects.name: Precision, Exploration and Guidance

skills.description: Precision is the confidence the agent assigns to a signal: high precision sharpens a distribution and lets it dominate an update, low precision flattens it and defers to other evidence. The same construct appears as sensory-precision weighting of prediction errors and as the policy precision that sharpens action selection, which is why precision, not a new mechanism each time, unifies attention and decision confidence.
skills.name: Precision as Confidence and Uncertainty Control

skills.description: Lowering the policy precision keeps the policy posterior high-entropy, which spreads probability across actions and produces exploration; raising it concentrates mass on the lowest-expected-free-energy policy and produces exploitation. Read this way the precision term plays the role of an entropy regulariser, the active-inference analogue of an exploration bonus in reinforcement learning.
skills.name: Entropy Regularisation and Exploration Bonuses

skills.description: Expected free energy already contains both an epistemic term that rewards uncertainty-reducing actions and a pragmatic term that rewards preferred outcomes, so an active-inference agent does not need a bolt-on exploration heuristic. The balance shifts with residual uncertainty: when the world is ambiguous the epistemic term dominates and the agent gathers information, and as uncertainty resolves the pragmatic term takes over and the agent pursues its goals.
skills.name: The Exploration–Exploitation Frontier

skills.description: The guidance view decomposes the pragmatic part of expected free energy into a risk term, the divergence between predicted and preferred outcomes, and an ambiguity term, the expected uncertainty of the likelihood. Shaping the preference distribution C is therefore how a designer steers behaviour: tightening C makes the policy risk-averse about deviating from goals, while flattening it tolerates a wider band of outcomes.
skills.name: Guidance Functions and Risk-Sensitive Policies

skills.description: Rate-distortion theory asks for the least information an agent must keep to hold expected distortion below a bound; expected free energy makes the mirror trade-off, balancing the epistemic value of an observation against the pragmatic value of a preferred outcome. Both say a bounded agent should pay for information only to the extent it buys reduced cost, which is why precision behaves like the slope that sets the exchange rate between bits gathered and value pursued.
skills.name: Rate-Distortion and the Epistemic-Pragmatic Trade-Off

subjects.description: Bayesian model reduction, structured vs mean-field approximations, sparse transition structure, and the exact VFE / log-evidence bound gap.
subjects.name: Model Reduction, Structure and Bound Tightness

skills.description: Bayesian model reduction evaluates how the free energy of an already-fitted model would change under a simpler (more precise or zeroed) prior, without re-fitting. Because the likelihood is unchanged, the evidence difference is a closed-form function of the posterior and the two priors, so many candidate reductions can be scored cheaply to prune redundant parameters and recover a sparser model.
skills.name: Bayesian Model Reduction

skills.description: A mean-field posterior factorises completely and so cannot represent correlations between latent variables; a structured (or marginal) approximation keeps chosen dependency edges, reducing the bound gap where those correlations matter at the cost of more expensive updates. Choosing the factorisation is itself a modelling decision about which posterior couplings are worth paying for.
skills.name: Structured vs Mean-Field Approximations

skills.description: When a transition model factorises across hidden-state factors, the joint update decomposes into smaller per-factor updates, and zeros in the dependency structure remove terms from the variational objective entirely. Sparsity is therefore not just a storage saving: it is the conditional-independence structure that makes message passing and model reduction tractable at scale.
skills.name: Sparse and Factorised Transition Structure

skills.description: The gap between variational free energy and the negative log-evidence is exactly the divergence between the approximate posterior and the true posterior, so the bound is tight precisely when that divergence vanishes. Tracking the gap turns 'is my approximation good enough?' into a measurable quantity: a structured approximation earns its cost only if it shrinks this gap where it matters.
skills.name: Bound Tightness: the VFE–Evidence Gap

subjects.description: Generalized coordinates of motion, embedding discrete decisions in continuous dynamics, and multi-scale temporal hierarchies.
subjects.name: Continuous-Time and Generalized-Coordinate AIF

skills.description: In continuous-time active inference a state is tracked together with its velocity, acceleration, and higher derivatives — a point in generalized coordinates of motion. Beliefs become trajectories rather than instantaneous estimates, and prediction errors are computed at each order, which is what lets a predictive-coding agent anticipate smooth dynamics instead of reacting to samples one at a time. Even at a single order the mechanism is exact for the linear-Gaussian case: descending the free energy along precision-weighted prediction errors settles the estimate at 1.33333, the analytic posterior mean, where the sensory error 0.666667 and the prior error 1.33333 balance once weighted by their precisions.
skills.name: Generalized Coordinates of Motion

skills.description: Mixed models couple a discrete active-inference layer that selects policies to a continuous layer that realises them: the discrete outcome supplies a prior over continuous setpoints, and the continuous layer's evidence feeds back as a likelihood for the discrete states. The interface is the place where symbolic decisions and smooth control have to agree on a shared free-energy accounting.
skills.name: Embedding Discrete Decisions in Continuous Dynamics

skills.description: Deep temporal models separate timescales: a high level that changes slowly supplies empirical priors to a faster low level, so context set higher up constrains moment-to-moment inference below. Free energy decomposes across levels and timescales, and the same minimisation that updates a fast percept also slowly revises the context that framed it — the structural basis of planning over nested horizons.
skills.name: Multi-Scale Temporal Hierarchies

subjects.description: Measure spaces, transport, identifiability and compositional modelling. It groups concepts that learners reuse directly in later strata and in the SkillTree learning path.
subjects.name: Frontier Mathematical Foundations

skills.description: A measure space separates the set of possible states from the sigma-algebra of events that can be assigned probability. This is the precise substrate for continuous generative models and prevents informal densities from being treated as if they were always ordinary functions.
skills.name: Measure Spaces for Generative Models

skills.description: Disintegration gives a rigorous version of conditioning in continuous spaces: a joint law can be decomposed into a marginal law and a conditional kernel. This is the measure-theoretic backbone of hierarchical generative models.
skills.name: Disintegration and Conditional Kernels

skills.description: Optimal transport compares distributions through the cost of moving mass between them. It complements KL-based geometry by remaining meaningful when supports barely overlap, which is useful for studying belief dynamics and mode movement.
skills.name: Optimal Transport and Distribution Geometry

skills.description: A model can only support action when hidden causes are observable enough to infer and controllable enough to influence. Identifiability asks whether distinct parameters imply distinguishable observation laws. These concepts expose when free-energy minimisation lacks the information needed to succeed.
skills.name: Observability, Controllability and Identifiability

skills.description: Category-theoretic language treats models as objects with explicit interfaces and transformations as structure-preserving maps. Used carefully, it clarifies how blankets, policies and messages can be composed across scales without silently changing what each component means.
skills.name: Compositional Models and Category-Theoretic Glue

subjects.description: Exchangeability, graphical models, interventions, filtering and nonparametric priors. It groups concepts that learners reuse directly in later strata and in the SkillTree learning path.
subjects.name: Frontier Probability & Causality

skills.description: Exchangeability means the order of observations does not matter to their joint law. It is weaker than independence and supports latent-variable explanations where observations are conditionally independent given a hidden parameter.
skills.name: Exchangeability and De Finetti Structure

skills.description: Directed and undirected graphical models make independence assumptions visible. For active inference, this clarifies which hidden factors, outcomes and policies can be updated locally and which dependencies require coupled messages.
skills.name: Graphical Models beyond Chains

skills.description: Causal graphs distinguish seeing from doing. Conditioning updates beliefs after an observation; intervention changes the generative process itself. This matters for active inference because policies are interventions, not passive evidence.
skills.name: Causal Graphs and Interventions

skills.description: Filtering estimates the current hidden state from past and present observations; smoothing revises past states using later observations; prediction projects future observations. Discrete active inference reuses all three operations inside policy evaluation.
skills.name: Filtering, Smoothing and Prediction

skills.description: Nonparametric Bayesian models place priors over flexible structures such as clusters, functions or state spaces. They are useful when the agent should be able to discover that its current catalogue of hidden causes is incomplete.
skills.name: Nonparametric Priors and Growing State Spaces

subjects.description: Description length, predictive efficiency, decomposition and semantic information. It groups concepts that learners reuse directly in later strata and in the SkillTree learning path.
subjects.name: Frontier Information Theory

skills.description: Minimum description length treats learning as compression: a good model gives a short joint code for the model plus the data under that model. This reframes Occam factors in evidence and free energy as penalties for wasteful structure.
skills.name: Minimum Description Length

skills.description: Predictive efficiency asks whether memory keeps information that helps predict future observations instead of merely memorising the past. It sharpens the distinction between epistemic value and indiscriminate data accumulation.
skills.name: Predictive Efficiency and Retained Information

skills.description: Partial information decomposition asks whether sources carry the same evidence, different evidence, or evidence that only appears when combined. It is a useful lens for multi-agent sensing, communication, and collective inference.
skills.name: Partial Information Decomposition

skills.description: An active sensor does not merely receive a channel; it configures the channel by moving, probing or querying. Expected free energy can therefore be read as a criterion for selecting informative channels under preference constraints.
skills.name: Active Sensing as Channel Design

skills.description: Semantic information is information that changes viable action, not just any posterior detail. In active inference this keeps epistemic value tied to the agent's generative model, preferences and policy repertoire.
skills.name: Semantic Information and Action-Relevance

subjects.description: Black-box gradients, flows, local projections, weighted bounds and streaming updates.
subjects.name: Frontier Variational Methods

skills.description: Black-box variational inference estimates gradients of the variational objective without deriving bespoke coordinate updates. It expands active-inference-style modelling to generative models whose posteriors are too complex for closed-form message passing.
skills.name: Black-Box Variational Inference

skills.description: A normalising flow transforms a simple base distribution into a flexible density while tracking the change in volume. As a recognition density, it can reduce the mismatch imposed by a rigid mean-field approximation.
skills.name: Normalising Flows as Recognition Densities

skills.description: Expectation propagation updates one factor at a time, then projects the result back into an approximating family. It highlights the design choice behind any message-passing scheme: what information is preserved when local beliefs are compressed.
skills.name: Expectation Propagation and Local Projections

skills.description: Importance-weighted bounds replace a single-sample estimate with a weighted set of samples. They can tighten the training objective, but they also expose the variance and degeneracy issues that appear when proposal and target diverge.
skills.name: Importance-Weighted Bounds

skills.description: Streaming variational inference maintains an approximate posterior as data arrive. It is the variational analogue of online perception and is essential when an agent must learn continually from a non-stationary stream.
skills.name: Streaming Variational Inference

subjects.description: Particular blankets, trajectory objectives, synchrony, autonomy and scale separation. It groups concepts that learners reuse directly in later strata and in the SkillTree learning path.
subjects.name: Frontier Free Energy Principle

skills.description: A particular blanket is not just a boundary in space; it is a modelling claim about which internal, external, sensory and active states form a system. The same physical process can be individuated differently depending on the inferential question.
skills.name: Particular Blankets and System Individuation

skills.description: Many organisms minimise surprise over trajectories, not isolated instants. A path-integral view treats histories as the objects of inference and makes the temporal structure of action, learning and self-maintenance explicit.
skills.name: Path Integrals and Trajectory Free Energy

skills.description: Generalised synchrony means one system's states become a lawful function of another's states. In FEP language, it clarifies how internal states can track external causes through a blanket while preserving their own dynamics.
skills.name: Generalised Synchrony and Coupled Systems

skills.description: Operational autonomy is the capacity of a system to keep itself within a viable set of states through action. The free-energy principle becomes concrete when viability constraints are stated as the outcomes the organism must keep sampling.
skills.name: Operational Autonomy and Viability

skills.description: FEP models become clearer when fast hidden-state inference, slower parameter learning and slow structural revision are not conflated. Scale separation explains why perception, adaptation and development need different update rules.
skills.name: Scale Separation across States, Parameters and Structure

subjects.description: Affordances, counterfactual policies, multifactor planning and open-ended exploration. It groups concepts that learners reuse directly in later strata and in the SkillTree learning path.
subjects.name: Frontier Active Inference

skills.description: An affordance field maps situations to action possibilities. In active inference, affordances are not merely perceived objects; they are predictions about which policies can reduce expected free energy from the current state.
skills.name: Affordance Fields

skills.description: Policy selection depends on counterfactual futures: what observations, beliefs and outcomes would follow if a policy were chosen. This makes planning a disciplined form of imagination constrained by the generative model.
skills.name: Counterfactual Policy Evaluation

skills.description: Factorised state spaces make planning tractable by decomposing hidden causes, but good policies still respect dependencies between factors. Multifactor planning tracks which parts of the policy tree can be evaluated independently.
skills.name: Multifactor Planning under Factorised State Spaces

skills.description: Agents can learn not only beliefs, but also the precision policies that determine which errors deserve attention. Meta-precision learning connects attention, confidence, habits and psychopathology in a single control problem.
skills.name: Meta-Precision Learning

skills.description: Some uncertainty cannot be resolved inside the current state space. Open-ended exploration recognises when the agent should add hypotheses, factors or actions rather than merely estimate existing variables more precisely.
skills.name: Open-Ended Exploration and Model Expansion

subjects.description: Schema validation, live seeding, replay, observability and local secret hygiene.
subjects.name: Frontier Implementation & Operations

skills.description: A generated artifact should be treated as untrusted until it passes schema and semantic checks. For SkillTree exports this means validating required fields, identifier formats and dependency endpoints before the dashboard reports the data as available.
skills.name: Schema Validation for Learning Artifacts

skills.description: A live seeder must be idempotent without becoming permissive. It should create subjects, skills, quizzes and dependencies in dependency-safe order, then query the server to verify that the live graph count equals the export.
skills.name: Batch Seeding and Idempotent Repair

skills.description: A replay harness records seeds, inputs, policies and observations so an agent trajectory can be rerun. This makes stochastic active-inference simulations auditable rather than anecdotal.
skills.name: Replay Harnesses for Agent Simulations

skills.description: The local dashboard should report whether artifacts are current, whether SkillTree is reachable, and whether local token exchange is ready. It must not become a second learning-state authority.
skills.name: Dashboard Observability without Reimplementing SkillTree

skills.description: Local helper servers can improve ergonomics, but secret-bearing token exchange must remain server-side and loopback-only. Serving a trusted-client bridge on a non-loopback host turns a development convenience into an authentication risk.
skills.name: Runtime Secret Hygiene for Local Tooling

subjects.description: Digital support, adaptive tutoring, teaming, urban sensing and institutional design.
subjects.name: Frontier Applications & Institutions

skills.description: Digital mental health systems can be evaluated as loops that sense context, infer latent need, choose interventions and update support policies. The hard part is calibrating precision and safety constraints, not merely increasing engagement.
skills.name: Digital Mental Health and Precision Support

skills.description: An adaptive tutor maintains beliefs about the learner's misconceptions and chooses questions, explanations and practice that are both epistemic for the tutor and useful for the learner.
skills.name: Adaptive Tutoring as Active Inference

skills.description: Human-robot teams require more than individual control. Each partner must infer what the other believes, can do and intends to do, then choose policies that keep the shared task legible and safe.
skills.name: Human-Robot Teaming and Shared Belief

skills.description: An urban sensing system decides which signals to sample, where to place attention and how to aggregate local observations into a city-scale posterior. This is an active-inference problem whenever sensing choices change future uncertainty.
skills.name: Urban Sensing and Collective Prediction

skills.description: Institutions allocate attention, define trusted evidence channels and constrain policy repertoires. Designing them as epistemic infrastructure connects cognitive security, collective active inference and practical governance.
skills.name: Institutional Design as Epistemic Infrastructure

subjects.description: Dimension checks, assumption checklists and sensitivity probes for validating the formal machinery before it is reused downstream.
subjects.name: Mathematical Model-Checking Practice

skills.description: A shape mismatch is often the earliest visible sign that a generative model has confused states, observations, actions or parameters. Learners practice reading each symbol through its domain, codomain and role in the update equation before trusting any optimisation step.
skills.name: Dimension Checks for Generative Models

skills.description: Many active-inference derivations silently rely on smooth objectives, valid probability simplices, or convex approximations. This skill trains learners to write the assumptions beside the calculation so later failures are diagnosable instead of mysterious.
skills.name: Assumption Checklists for Derivations

skills.description: Taylor, Laplace and gradient-based approximations can look precise while hiding sensitivity to curvature and update size. Learners vary the local assumptions and explain whether the same qualitative inference still holds.
skills.name: Sensitivity Probes for Approximation Errors

subjects.description: Story-to-factorisation, missing-data handling and prior predictive checks for turning scenarios into inspectable probabilistic models.
subjects.name: Probabilistic Modelling Practice

skills.description: Before a learner can perform Bayesian inference, they must decide what the model claims exists and how those variables depend on one another. This skill turns a narrative into an explicit factorisation that can be checked and revised.
skills.name: From Story to Probabilistic Factorisation
